upstream.sha_note: commit target of tag v0.3.5; submodule pointers are commits, not annotated tag objects

upstream_choice.summary: elixir-lang/tree-sitter-elixir is not one option among several: it is the grammar, it lives in the language's own GitHub org, and all three editors ship it. They pin three DIFFERENT commits, and it does not matter -- across all three pins and the released tag the parser inputs are byte-identical.
upstream_choice.evidence: nvim-treesitter parsers.lua -> elixir-lang/tree-sitter-elixir @ 4b0c7118 (HEAD, 2026-07-20); Helix languages.toml [[grammar]] name="elixir" -> same repo @ 7937d3b4 (2026-03-13); Zed's extension moved out of the zed repo to zed-extensions/elixir, whose extension.toml [grammars.elixir] -> same repo @ 450a8194 (2025-03-03). VERIFIED rather than assumed: `git rev-parse <sha>:grammar.js` and `<sha>:src/scanner.c` return the SAME two blobs (ba722b212c, 9e744a1eb0) for all three editor pins AND for the v0.3.5 tag pinned here -- 17 months in which the parser did not change at all. The four commits between v0.3.5 and HEAD touch bindings/c, bindings/go, go.mod, .gitignore and queries/injections.scm, i.e. nothing tree-sitter generate reads.
upstream_choice.why_the_tag_and_not_head: The tag is what crates.io's tree-sitter-elixir 0.3.5 is (3,028,244 downloads all-time, 1,212,401 recent -- the 3.0 M figure the roadmap ranked on), so upstream.version means the same thing to a consumer as it does here. Pinning HEAD would buy an injections query and a pkg-config file, and cost a version string that names no release.
upstream_choice.alternatives_considered: There is no second Elixir grammar with a following. The one adjacent grammar is tree-sitter-heex (phoenixframework), which Zed pins BESIDE this one for .heex templates; HEEx embeds Elixir rather than being Elixir, so it is a separate grammar for a separate language and is not vendored here. See the classify() note in crates/treebank-cli/src/lang/elixir.rs.

generate_cli_note: same pin as the other grammars: tree-sitter-cli 0.26.x ships broken Unicode identifier tables (see treebank-rust ledger)

toolchain.summary: Two grammars sit on the BEAM -- this one and erlang (roadmap #18), whose oracle epp_dodger lives in OTP's own syntax_tools. The toolchain is therefore installed by tools/beam-toolchain/fetch.sh rather than by anything Elixir-specific, and `--otp-only` is the half an Erlang session needs.
toolchain.source: builds.hex.pm, the Hex team's build host and the one erlef/setup-beam pulls from. OTP is published there per distribution, so ubuntu-24.04 is a build against this box's OpenSSL and ncurses. Both artifacts are checksummed in fetch.sh against builds.txt.
toolchain.cost: 77 MB of OTP plus 8.6 MB of Elixir; 3.6 s from nothing to a working iex on a warm network. Building OTP from source (kerl/asdf, the usual path) is 10-20 minutes for the same result.
toolchain.why_not_the_distribution: Ubuntu 24.04 ships Elixir 1.14.0 on OTP 25, both from 2022. The oracle version IS the dialect, so three years of parser changes is not a rounding error. Erlang Solutions' apt repo (binaries2.erlang-solutions.com) is not reachable from this box's proxy; builds.hex.pm is.

oracle.tool: tools/elixir-oracle/check.exs, run under elixir (TREEBANK_ELIXIR names the binary when it is not on PATH)
oracle.note: Elixir's own front end via Code.string_to_quoted/2 -- the call the compiler makes to turn a file's text into an AST. TWO-VALUED: valid / invalid. It tokenizes and parses and stops: no macro expansion, no use/import/require resolution, no module attribute evaluation, no .exs execution, so a missing dependency is not an error and each file is judged on its own text. check.exs refuses to run under a different Elixir MINOR rather than silently producing verdicts for an unrecorded dialect; an OTP mismatch warns instead of refusing, because the parser is Elixir code while OTP underneath supplies the runtime and the Unicode tables.
oracle.unreadable_note: An unreadable file is NOT an invalid file: the oracle writes the path and reason to stderr and exits 1 rather than emitting a verdict, so a mistyped corpus root fails the sweep instead of turning every grammar failure into noise and reporting a flawless grammar. Verified after the fact: a nonexistent path and a directory (which opens cleanly on Linux and fails only on read, with :eisdir) are each fatal rather than 'invalid'.

smoke.note: check.exs is a BATCH oracle — one long-lived VM for the whole run — so a bug in it does not fail one file, it votes on all of them, and its first draft did exactly that: a mistyped option raised, a blanket rescue caught it, and every file came back `invalid`. Assertion (2), that a known-valid file still comes back valid, is what catches that shape. `requires` names the bare command because tools/beam-toolchain/fetch.sh puts the pinned Elixir on PATH; TREEBANK_ELIXIR still overrides which binary runs.

oracle_does_not_evaluate.summary: VERIFIED, not assumed. Elixir runs arbitrary code at COMPILE time -- module bodies, module attributes, macros, `use` -- and this oracle is pointed at thousands of strangers' files, so 'it only parses' had to be measured before a single file was swept.
oracle_does_not_evaluate.battery: Six adversarial fixtures: (1) a module body calling File.write! and System.cmd; (2) a module attribute bound to File.read! of an absent path plus an immediately-invoked fn writing a file; (3) a defmacro with a side effect in its body, plus a second module doing require/import/use on it and calling it; (4) a top-level .exs running File.write!, System.cmd, :os.cmd, Code.eval_string and spawn; (5) sigil and string interpolation wrapping a side effect; (6) compile-time `if` and `for` comprehension writing files.
oracle_does_not_evaluate.result: Parsed through Code.string_to_quoted/2: zero files written, zero subprocesses, zero spawned processes, BEAM process count unchanged before and after.
oracle_does_not_evaluate.control: The result means nothing without this half. COMPILING and RUNNING the same six files produces TEN side-effect markers (Code.compile_file for the .ex files, elixir for the .exs). The battery fires when it should; it simply never fires through the parse path.
oracle_does_not_evaluate.why_this_matters_more_here_than_elsewher: python's compile(), ts.createSourceFile and javac -proc:none are parse-only because their languages have no compile-time execution to speak of. Elixir does, and it is the language's headline feature. This is the closest any treebank oracle has come to the Tier-C disqualifier 'the parser executes the corpus', and the answer is that Code.string_to_quoted/2 sits strictly BELOW the layer where that starts.

oracle_cost.headline: 1.35 s per 1000 files over the full 9,423-file / 104.7 MB corpus (12.7 s), and 1.02 s per 1000 on a 1,000-file subset. Firmly Tier A.
oracle_cost.decomposition: 0.49 s is fixed VM startup, paid once per batch (bare `erl` is 0.20 s of that; Elixir's own boot adds ~0.3 s). Parsing runs at 8.5-9.4 MB/s, so seconds-per-1000-FILES tracks corpus composition rather than the oracle: the same script measures 0.65 s/1000 on a 3,359-file top-200 sample averaging 6.0 KB/file, against 1.30 s/1000 here where the mean is 11.1 KB. Peak RSS 505 MB on the full corpus, 126 MB on the smaller sample.
oracle_cost.reject_path: 0.70 s per 1000 with every file truncated to 60% of its length -- the input validate() actually sees -- against 1.35 on the valid path. Roughly 1.9x faster, the same shape rust's syn and go/parser show: the parser bails at the first error instead of recovering. (Per byte it is only ~1.15x, since the truncated corpus is 60% of the bytes.)
oracle_cost.roadmap_comparison: The roadmap lists elixir as Tier A with this oracle but never measured a cost, so the only figure to disagree with is the Tier A band, 0.2-2 s per 1000. The measured number sits mid-band, beside python (1.23) and rust (1.28). NO DISAGREEMENT -- but see oracle_not_fork_per_file, because that tier is a property of the implementation and not of the language.

oracle_not_fork_per_file.summary: The obvious implementation is a fork per file, the way `php -l` and `bash -n` MUST work. Measured: `elixir -e` per file is 31.2 s for 100 files, i.e. 312 s per 1000 -- 9x worse than libclang's 35.5 and a third of the way to C++'s 1068. That implementation would move the roadmap's easiest Tier-A oracle out of Tier A entirely.
oracle_not_fork_per_file.batched: One long-lived VM reading paths on stdin: 0.51 s for the same 100 files, 1.35 s per 1000 over the full corpus. A 325x swing that lives entirely in the harness.
oracle_not_fork_per_file.why_the_swing_is_so_large_here: Elixir has the largest fixed startup of any Tier-A oracle in this repo -- 0.49 s against bash's 2.0 ms and php's 15 ms -- so a fork-per-file design throws away half a second PER FILE. php and bash had no choice (a forked interpreter is the only way to syntax-check a file with those tools); this one does, and taking it needs no parallel driver and nothing to tune.
oracle_not_fork_per_file.recorded_because: The php ledger records a batch oracle it built and REJECTED on correctness grounds. This is the mirror case: the batch form is not merely faster, it is the only form that keeps the tier the roadmap assigned, and it is correct for the plain reason that Code.string_to_quoted/2 is a pure function of one file's bytes.

oracle_blanket_rescue_trap.summary: The first draft of check.exs returned 'invalid' for all 3,359 files in the sample corpus, and looked like it was working.
oracle_blanket_rescue_trap.cause: It passed `column: true` where Elixir spells the option `columns:`. That raises FunctionClauseError deep inside :elixir_compiler -- and a blanket `rescue -> "invalid"` caught it and voted.
oracle_blanket_rescue_trap.consequence_if_it_had_shipped: Every grammar failure adjudicated as corpus NOISE, gap_files 0, and a sweep report saying the grammar is flawless. Exactly the failure GRAMMARS.md names ('an unreadable file is not an invalid file') arriving through a door that note does not cover: not I/O, but an oracle BUG.
oracle_blanket_rescue_trap.fix: The rescue is one exception wide. UnicodeConversionError is the only thing measured to escape as an exception, raised on bytes that are not UTF-8 -- a verdict about content, since Elixir source is UTF-8 by definition. Everything else was probed and returns {:error, _} cleanly: hand-written garbage, a lone NUL byte, unterminated strings and heredocs, a byte order mark, 20,000-deep parenthesis nesting, a 50,000-element list, and 4 KB of random bytes. An oracle bug must crash, not vote.

oracle_atom_table.summary: A long-lived BEAM interns an atom for every new identifier it parses, and the atom table is bounded (1,048,576 by default) and never garbage collected. Measured: +38,342 atoms over 3,359 files, ~11 per file, sublinear -- a second pass over the same files adds ZERO, because the growth is bounded by the corpus's vocabulary rather than by its file count. That is ~87,000 unfamiliar files of headroom in one process.
oracle_atom_table.why_it_does_not_bite: validate() only ever runs on files the grammar already failed -- 1 file in this sweep, tens to hundreds on a bad day -- and each sweep spawns a fresh VM. The ceiling is not reachable on the real workload.
oracle_atom_table.the_fix_if_it_ever_does: Code.string_to_quoted/2 takes a :static_atoms_encoder. Measured with one: ZERO atoms created, IDENTICAL verdicts on all 3,359 files, and marginally faster (0.55 vs 0.60 s/1000). It is deliberately not enabled, because it changes what the parser builds for no benefit on the real input size; recorded here so the option and its measured equivalence are not rediscovered from scratch.

grammar_is_broader_than_the_oracle.summary: The grammar accepts a small class of files Elixir's parser rejects. This runs in the SAFE direction -- grammar accepts, oracle rejects -- so it can never manufacture a gap, and gap_files stays exact. It matters because it bounds what test/negative/ may contain.
grammar_is_broader_than_the_oracle.measured: Of a 27-file adversarial battery that Code.string_to_quoted/2 rejects, the grammar rejects 23 and accepts 4: a byte order mark before valid code, invalid UTF-8 bytes inside a string, a stray `end` at top level, and a map with no => between key and value (%{a b}).
grammar_is_broader_than_the_oracle.why: Three of the four are lexical facts a tree-sitter grammar does not model -- a BOM is just a codepoint to it, invalid UTF-8 is replaced rather than rejected, and neither is expressible in grammar.js. The other two are parser-level: Elixir's own parser tracks do/end nesting and map syntax more strictly than the LR grammar does.
grammar_is_broader_than_the_oracle.negative_corpus_consequence: test/negative/ contains only failures BOTH sides agree on: 23 files, each verified rejected by the grammar (via `treebank negative`, the same check CI runs) AND by the oracle. The four above are deliberately excluded -- a negative test built from them would be testing the modelling gap, not the grammar, and would fail forever.

corpus.source: Hex package tarballs (repo.hex.pm) for the top packages by recent downloads.
corpus.ranking_note: First-party and free, unlike PyPI (an external BigQuery extract) and LuaRocks (scraped HTML). The metric is downloads.recent -- RECENT rather than all-time, the opposite bias to LuaRocks' cumulative count: it favours what is in use now over what was downloaded once. A large share of Hex traffic is CI re-resolving transitive dependencies, so the top of the list leans toward small libraries everything depends on rather than toward applications. The listing endpoint also carries latest_stable_version per package, so version resolution costs no extra request; packages that have only ever published pre-releases fall back to latest_version rather than being dropped.
corpus.hex_is_not_an_elixir_registry: It is the BEAM's registry, and Erlang packages rank alongside Elixir ones. MEASURED over the top 500: 107 packages (21.4%) contain no .ex/.exs file at all -- ranch, idna, cowlib, certifi, cowboy, hackney and the rest are Erlang. They are fetched and contribute nothing. Filtering them would need a per-release request for meta.build_tools (the listing endpoint does not carry it) to save a few megabytes, and those same packages are the entire point of this corpus for the erlang grammar that comes next.
corpus.archive_shape: A Hex tarball is TWO archives: name-version.tar is an uncompressed tar holding VERSION, CHECKSUM, metadata.config and contents.tar.gz, and the source is one level down. Two consequences in fetch.rs. (1) Lang::nested_archives, built by lua for the quarter of .src.rock files carrying upstream's tarball whole, is needed here for EVERY package -- so every corpus path carries the nested prefix contents.tar.gz/. Kept rather than special-cased: it is true, and the alternative is a new trait hook that exists to make one registry's paths prettier. (2) Lang::archive_strip returns 0, because the outer tar's four members are single-component names; the default of one component for a tar would strip them to nothing and every package would extract EMPTY, silently, since an empty package is not an error anywhere.
corpus.uncompressed_tar: Hex is the first registry here to ship an UNCOMPRESSED tar. fetch.rs sniffed six magic bytes and fell through to gzip for anything it did not recognise -- right by accident for every previous registry, and `invalid gzip header` on the first Hex package. Fixed by reading 264 bytes and checking for POSIX's `ustar` at offset 257, in shape(), decompress() and decompress_bytes() alike; the cached file is also named .tar rather than .tar.gz now.
corpus.files_note: .ex and .exs, the two extensions tree-sitter-elixir's tree-sitter.json claims, both parsed by the one grammar -- the difference is that .exs is evaluated rather than compiled, a runtime distinction with no syntax behind it. So mix.exs, .formatter.exs and test files are in the corpus, and should be: that is where a package's more unusual syntax tends to live (726 of the 9,423 files are .exs). .heex and .eex are excluded: they are template languages that EMBED Elixir, they have their own grammar (tree-sitter-heex, which Zed pins beside this one), and feeding them here would manufacture failures out of files that are not Elixir.
corpus.fetched: 2026-08-13 (hex.pm rankings and tarballs of that date)

patches.title: treebank redistribution notice
patches.origin: treebank; README warning that this tree is a generated, patched redistribution (treebank.dev), applied first so every materialized tree carries it

patches.title: treebank crate identity
patches.origin: treebank; upstream owns the tree-sitter-elixir name on crates.io, so the redistribution publishes under its own: package name, repository, homepage and description. [lib] name is pinned to tree_sitter_elixir so the crate stays a drop-in replacement -- upstream declares no [lib] name at all and relies on the package name, so renaming the package without this would rename the library too. include gains LOCAL-PATCHES.md, ledger.json and patches/* so provenance travels inside the published tarball. Upstream ships no Cargo.lock, so unlike lua this patch touches Cargo.toml alone. The published version string is deliberately NOT here: publish.sh derives it from crates.io at publish time. See PUBLISHING.md.
patches.note: Also adds NOTICE to the include list. tree-sitter-elixir is Apache-2.0 and ships a NOTICE file, which section 4(d) requires every redistribution to carry -- and it is not decorative: it is where the MIT terms for the tree-sitter-generated files in src/ (Max Brunsfeld) and for the test/corpus fragments (Anantha Kumaran) are stated. Upstream's include list names only LICENSE, so the crate published on crates.io today ships neither. Fixed here rather than left for upstream, exactly like lua's LICENSE/LICENSE.md correction, and worth offering upstream as a standalone one-line fix. tree-sitter.json is added for the same reason: upstream omits it and it carries the grammar's own version and file-type metadata.

patches.title: backslash pair before a non-interpolating end delimiter
patches.origin: treebank; found by this crate's first Hex sweep. NOT previously reported upstream -- elixir-lang/tree-sitter-elixir was searched for backslash, escape and sigil issues and PRs and has none covering it -- so this is ours to offer upstream.

evidence.diagnosis: scan_quoted_content ends the content token as soon as it sees a backslash whose NEXT character is the end delimiter, so the grammar's escape_sequence rule can consume the escaped delimiter. Right for `~S(\)`, which really is unterminated. But it never accounts for a backslash that was itself escaped: in `~S(\\)` the scanner consumes the first backslash, loops, sees the second with `)` behind it and stops -- so the grammar reads `\)` as an escaped delimiter and the sigil never closes. The fix consumes the PAIR when a backslash follows a backslash in a non-interpolating form. Interpolating forms were never affected: there the scanner returns after ANY backslash and the grammar's full escape_sequence rule consumes `\\` as one token, which is why `~s(\\)` always parsed and `~S(\\)` never did.
evidence.boundary: An ODD number of backslashes before the delimiter really does escape it and must still fail. Verified for all eight delimiter pairs: `~S(\)` invalid/rejected, `~S(\\)` valid/now parses, `~S(\\\)` invalid/still rejected, `~S(\\\\)` valid/now parses. Heredocs take a different branch (a backslash before a newline is deliberately ignored so the end delimiter stays recognisable) and were unaffected in both directions. The odd case is pinned by test/negative/escaped-end-delimiter-sigil.ex and by the consumer test's must-reject.ex so a later 'improvement' cannot quietly widen the fix onto it.
evidence.semantics_checked: Against the real tokenizer rather than assumed: ~S(\\) evaluates to a TWO-character string, so both backslashes are content and neither is dropped -- which is exactly what consuming the pair produces.
evidence.evidence_note: One file in 9,423 and zero regressions, both measured over the identical corpus with only this patch removed and restored. Upstream's own corpus tests go 302 -> 303 (the new case) with highlight and tag parses unchanged at 293/293; the 23-file negative corpus is still fully rejected; the sweep's noise count does not move.
evidence.upstream_status: unreported; offer as a PR against elixir-lang/tree-sitter-elixir
